title: Electrode Interface Effects in Hafnium Zirconium Oxide Ferroelectrics
content: Hafnium oxide-based ferroelectrics have garnered increased attention due to their high dielectric constant and potential use as non-volatile memory elements for CMOS integration [1-3]. Their superior physical properties, such as scalability under 15 nm thickness, make them promising candidates for advanced electronic applications [4, 5]. Despite these advantages, these materials exhibit retention loss and fatigue problems, which are influenced by the choice of electrode [6, 7]. This study aims to elucidate the effect of different electrodes, such as tantalum nitride (TaN) and tungsten (W), on the structural and electrical behavior of hafnium zirconium oxide films (HZO). The films were produced using a Metal-Ferroelectric-Metal architecture by plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition and sputtering, and characterized by advanced scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). The elemental distribution was analyzed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (STEM-EDS), while the local bonding environment and composition quantification were characterized through electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS). Structural characterization was performed at atomic resolution using STEM imaging techniques, including high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) and differentiated differential phase contrast (dDPC) imaging, as shown in Fig. 1. Phase identification was carried out using vector pair correlation functions (vPCF, shown in Fig. 2) combined with fast Fourier transform (FFT) analysis. Experimental EELS spectra were acquired through the thickness and compared with ab initio EELS simulations for different phases and orientations using FEFF10 [8]. Simulation parameters included an energy resolution of 0.2 eV and k-space sampling with a 25 mrad convergence angle, ensuring accurate spectral features for distinguishing between HZO polymorphs. Large supercells ensured convergence in real-space calculations, allowing systematic differentiation of polymorphs based on their O K-edge features. The findings highlight the critical role of electrode selection in mitigating reliability issues such as retention loss and fatigue, while also providing insights into distinguishing different polymorphs within these complex structures. By integrating high-resolution experimental techniques and computational approaches, this study provides insights into the interplay between electrode interfaces and phase heterogeneity in HZO, paving the way for enhanced design and performance of ferroelectric materials in electronic devices [9].
